Yes, smoking can increase the risk of developing Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). According to the CDC, "multiple studies show that cigarette smoking increases a person's risk of developing RA and can make the disease worse" [d1]. NIAMS similarly confirms that "people who smoke over a long period of time are at an increased risk of getting rheumatoid arthritis," and that continued smoking may make the disease more severe [d3]. A peer-reviewed BMJ study further notes that "cigarette smoking has been shown to increase the risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis," and that it interacts with genetic risk factors to produce an even greater risk [d4]. A comprehensive review identifies smoking as "one of the most established environmental risk factors for RA development and severity" and the only environmental factor "extensively studied and widely accepted" in this context [d6], with research also linking smoking to pathogenic mechanisms such as oxidative stress, inflammation, and epigenetic changes [d6], as well as alterations in citrullination of autoantigens [d5].
